newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open steady amid stock concerns.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open steady amid stock concerns.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened little changed in quiet trade on Tuesday, with concerns about recent sharp declines in equities continuing to provide support for the money market, analysts said.

"The concern is still very much what's happening in the the equity world and what could potentially happen in the mutual fund world," said one T-bill trader with a bank-owned brokerage. "People are starting to park a little bit more cash into the short end and staying in that area."
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill traded with a yield of 2.97 percent, unchanged from Monday's close.
Dealers said this morning's Canadian consumer price index report for July did not have a major impact on T-bill prices.

Canada's unadjusted July consumer price index rose 1.8. percent in the year, Statistics Canada said Tuesday. Core CPI rose 1.5 percent year-on-year. Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast a 1.8 percent year-over-year rise in the all-items index and a 1.9 percent increase in the core CPI.
Analysts said the data was likely to push back the timing of a second Bank of Canada rate hike this year, which would likely weigh on the Canadian dollar.

T-bill investors are now looking ahead to the results of the weekly Government of Canada T-bill tender later today. The Bank of Canada will sell C$4.2 billion of three-month, six-month and one-year T-bills, even as C$4.6 billion of T-bills fall due.

In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill traded unchanged from Monday to yield 3.52 percent. The one-year when-issued T-bill weakened to yield 3.96 percent from 3.95 percent. The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.25 percent, the center of the Bank of Canada's 3.0-3.5 percent target range.
